standard.title: Language to justify preferences
standard.description: explore language to provide reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explore different ways of using language to express preferences, likes and dislikes (AC9EFLA02). They have not yet used connective language such as 'because' to provide reasons, or comparative adjectives to express degrees of preference.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore language that provides reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences, including connective and comparative language.

nodes.label: Stating a preference
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can express a like, dislike or preference using appropriate language (e.g. 'I like...', 'I prefer...', 'My favourite is...').
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least two different language forms to express a preference or dislike.
nodes.typical_width: Express likes, dislikes and preferences using a range of language forms across different topic contexts — books, activities, foods, stories.
wider: Explore how preference language differs between informal speech and written opinion texts
Compare how characters in picture books or stories express preferences, identifying the language used
success_criteria: Student uses at least two different language forms to express a preference
Student applies preference language in a new context when prompted

nodes.label: Giving reasons with 'because'
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use 'because' and similar connectives to link a preference to a reason.
nodes.minimum_width: Construct at least one sentence using 'because' to give a reason for a preference or dislike.
nodes.typical_width: Use 'because' and similar connectives to provide reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences across a range of topics, with reasons that are specific to the preference stated.
wider: Explore other reason-giving connectives (e.g. 'since', 'as') and compare how they feel in spoken versus written contexts
Examine how reasons in opinion texts are structured, linking to AC9E1LA03 text organisation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who append comments rather than genuinely linking a reason with 'because' cannot produce the reasoned opinion required for AC9E1LY06 opinion writing — the connective structure is a prerequisite for coherent opinion text production.

response_modes.reason: Using 'because' to genuinely link a reason (not just append a comment) requires repeated practice. Students frequently produce 'I like dogs because dogs are nice' — consolidation builds the habit of a substantive, specific reason.

success_criteria: Student produces a sentence using 'because' where the reason is specific to the stated preference
Student can identify the reason part of a given 'because' sentence

nodes.label: Comparative language for degree
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use comparative adjectives to express the degree of a preference (e.g. 'better', 'faster', 'more exciting').
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one comparative adjective to express a preference and explain what it is comparing.
nodes.typical_width: Use comparative adjectives (including irregular forms like 'better') to express degrees of preference, naming what is being compared.
wider: Explore superlatives ('best', 'fastest') as an extension of comparative degree language
Investigate how comparative adjectives are used in advertising and persuasive texts to express preference or recommendation

response_modes.reason: Students often use comparatives without a clear referent ('it's better' — better than what?). Encountering comparatives across varied contexts — speech, picture books, advertising — helps establish that comparison requires two things to compare.

success_criteria: Student uses a comparative adjective correctly in a sentence expressing preference
Student identifies what two things are being compared in a given comparative sentence
